Island Pond.metaTitle: Island Pond, VT Wildlife Removal | Brighton & the Kingdom Lake
Island Pond.metaDescription: Beavers, bats, porcupines, and squirrels in Island Pond, VT — village homes and lake camps on Island Pond in the heart of the Northeast Kingdom. Same-day service — call us.
Island Pond.housing_era: The village of Island Pond in the town of Brighton, with older village homes and a small downtown, seasonal and year-round camps around the lake, and rural homes on the roads toward Newark, Charleston, and Morgan.
Island Pond.geographic_features: Island Pond lake (the lake at the center of the village, fed by the Clyde River), Clyde River (flows out of the pond west toward Newport), Nulhegan Basin (vast forest and wetland country to the south and east), Brighton State Park woods (forested parkland on the lake's southern shore)
neighborhoods: Island Pond village center (downtown and older village homes)

Island Pond.wildlife_intro:
Island Pond is deep Kingdom forest country, and its calls reflect camps and woods more than streets. Beavers dam culverts and flood camp roads around the pond and the Clyde River, porcupines and red squirrels work the camps all winter, and bats summer in camp attics and the village's older homes. Raccoons are steady around the lake, and fishers are a real concern for chicken keepers on the rural roads.

A camp here can sit snowed-in for months, so fall proofing and a careful spring opening are the rhythm our crew works to. Bat exclusion on camps and homes is timed for spring or late August through fall with one-way doors, winter is for proofing empty buildings, and no colony work happens while pups are flightless. Beaver flooding can happen fast in spring runoff — call us as soon as water starts rising where it should not.

faqs.q: Why are porcupines such a problem at Island Pond camps?
faqs.a: Camps offer salt-treated wood, plywood glues, and quiet all winter — everything a porcupine wants. One animal can damage several buildings in a season. Our crew removes problem animals lawfully and helps you shield vulnerable wood and store salt sources inside, which is what keeps the next porcupine from taking its place.

Concord.geographic_features: Connecticut River (forms the eastern border with New Hampshire), Moose River (flows through town to join the Connecticut), Miles Pond (camp pond in the western part of town), Nulhegan and Victory forest country (large wooded blocks to the north and west)

Concord.wildlife_intro:
Concord's wildlife work is beaver water, farm raccoons, and camp animals. Beavers flood fields, driveways, and town-road culverts along the Moose River and the valley brooks, raccoons and skunks work the Connecticut valley farms, and porcupines, red squirrels, and mice settle into Miles Pond camps and rural homes over the winter. Bats are common in the older farmhouses and barns along Route 2.

Spring runoff is beaver season here, and fall is proofing season for every camp and farmhouse that will sit quiet in a Kingdom winter. Summer bat colonies are exclusion only — one-way doors in spring and late August through November, proofing from December through March, and no colony work while pups cannot fly. Vermont prohibits relocating furbearers, so our crew explains the lawful options, including licensed trapping where it is needed, before any work starts.

faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much proofing or cleanup the building needs, so we do not quote a firm price before seeing the job. faqs.q: Can anything be done about beavers without removing them in Concord?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Where the site allows, a pond-leveling pipe can hold water at a level that protects a road or field while the beavers stay. Where flooding threatens a home, septic, or the only access road, trapping by a licensed trapper may be the honest answer. Our crew will assess the site and tell you which route fits.

Lunenburg.wildlife_intro:
Lunenburg splits between its hilltop village — older homes with attic bats, squirrels, and chimney raccoons — and Gilman's mill-era housing and river farms, where raccoons, skunks, and beavers along the Connecticut and its brooks are the steady calls. Porcupines and red squirrels trouble the rural homes and camps in the woods, and woodchucks work the open farm ground along Route 2 through the summer.

Winters on the hill are long and windy, and animals that get in during fall stay until spring, which is why our crew pushes proofing before the snow. Bat work follows the state pattern: exclusion with one-way doors in spring and late August through fall, full proofing in winter, and no colony work while pups are flightless. If a beaver dam is backing water toward your road or field, call us early — spring water moves fast.

faqs.q: Are bats common in Lunenburg's older village homes?
faqs.a: Yes. Tall, warm attics and small gaps at chimneys, eaves, and old trim make the hilltop homes easy roosts, and colonies return each summer. The lasting fix is whole-building proofing plus one-way doors at the active exits, timed outside the weeks when young bats cannot fly. Our crew inspects the full roofline so no secondary gap is left open.

Canaan.wildlife_intro:
Canaan is as remote as Vermont gets, and most calls come from camps, farms, and a compact village. Beavers flood woods roads and fields along Leach Creek and the young Connecticut, porcupines chew camps through the winter, and red squirrels and mice are constant in any building left quiet. Bats summer in village homes and farm barns, and raccoons work the river farms and village garages.

Distance and winter shape the work here — a camp may not be visited between fall and mud season, so proofing before closing is everything, and our crew schedules Canaan runs to check several properties in a trip when neighbors call together. Bat exclusion is timed for spring or late August through fall, with winter for proofing and no colony work while pups cannot fly. Call us in late summer if your camp needs closing up right.

faqs.q: How can I protect a remote Canaan camp that I rarely visit in winter?
faqs.a: Proof it hard in the fall: seal foundation and roofline gaps with chew-proof material, screen chimneys and vents, and remove food and salt sources porcupines seek. Our crew can do that closing work and check the building at opening. In deep-snow country, prevention is worth far more than a mid-winter emergency trip.
